risks.note: Blast furnace operations rely on a stable supply of low-ash met coke and domestic availability of prime grades remains limited, so a portion of requirements is directly or indirectly linked to imported met coke. Landed costs move with seaborne coking coal prices, freight, exchange rates and supplier-country exports; any sharp rise in global met coke prices or disruption in import flows can quickly raise hot metal cost and compress margins, especially when pig iron prices do not adjust in tandem. India's new definitive anti-dumping duties on low-ash met coke (reported at USD 42.95 to USD 128.83 per tonne) add to this cost exposure where domestic supply is insufficient in quantity and quality.
risks.risk: Dependence on low-ash metallurgical coke, largely import-linked

risks.note: The Company is exposed to fluctuations in iron ore, coke, limestone, power and logistics costs. Sudden increases in iron ore levies, changes in coal pricing, railway freight rationalisation or supply disruptions can materially alter the cost structure; because pig iron prices are largely set by broader steel cycles, the Company may not always be able to pass higher costs to customers immediately. Volatility in coking coal and iron ore is described as a persistent threat to production economics, swiftly eroding pig iron spreads when domestic realisations lag.
risks.risk: Raw material and energy price volatility with limited pass-through

risks.note: Despite moderation in finished steel imports, the domestic market remains vulnerable to low-priced material from surplus economies - particularly China and South-East Asia - during periods of weak global demand. Such inflows depress steel and pig iron realisations and narrow the spread between raw material and finished product prices; for a merchant pig iron producer, prolonged undercutting or aggressive competitor discounting can erode profitability even when volumes hold up.
risks.risk: Exposure to low-cost imports, dumping and price undercutting

risks.note: The industry is driven by global demand cycles, geopolitical developments and trade-policy changes. Slowdowns in major economies, unexpected shifts in Chinese steel output, or tariff changes in export markets affect sentiment and pricing for ferrous products; cyclicality in end-user industries such as construction, infrastructure and automotive directly impacts sales volumes and pricing power. Prolonged downturns or sharp price corrections could weigh on cash flows and delay planned investments. FY2025-26 already showed this - merchant mini blast furnace output moderated in H2 on weaker realisations and softer induction-furnace demand, and Durgapur steel-grade pig iron prices touched near five-year lows by October 2025.
risks.risk: Macro and industry cyclicality in pig iron and steel

risks.note: Regulators and customers are increasingly focused on emissions, energy efficiency and environmental performance across the iron and steel chain. Blast furnace based producers will be expected to adopt more efficient technologies, invest in energy savings and enhance monitoring and reporting - all of which carry capital and operating costs. The report explicitly flags that for a mid-sized company the pace and sequencing of such investments will need careful planning to avoid strain on the balance sheet. Emission norms and waste management standards are named among medium-to-long-term concerns.

currentContext.expansion: K I C Metaliks has expanded through a sequence of brownfield upgrades at its integrated eastern-India works rather than a new greenfield site. Following modernisation of its Mini Blast Furnace, which lifted hot metal production capacity to 165,000 MTPA, the Company over the last five years commissioned a Pulverized Coal Injection (PCI) system, a 25 sq.m Annular Sinter Plant 2 and an Oxygen Plant; these investments raised annual hot metal production capacity to 235,000 MTPA while improving operational efficiency, cost competitiveness and resource utilisation. Backward integration is anchored by an Annular Sinter Plant of 360,000 MTPA that converts iron ore fines and coke fines into sinter, and energy self-supply by a blast-furnace-gas based captive power plant of 4.7 MW that converts waste gases into steam for power. During FY2025-26 the Company undertook a series of operational initiatives aimed at productivity, reliability and cost efficiency - improvements in raw material handling infrastructure, process optimisation and efficiency-enhancing projects - and states that ongoing projects including raw material handling system enhancement, waste heat recovery initiatives and various other waste-to-wealth projects continue, aimed at improving productivity and reducing production costs. No new capacity addition, commissioning date or ramp timeline for a further expansion is disclosed in the routed text; the FY2025-26 gain came from utilisation (73.21% to 90.22%) on the existing asset base rather than from new capacity. Other installed enabling assets described are a coke drying system, oxygen and nitrogen gas plants, mechanised raw material handling, dust extraction and gas-cleaning equipment, and quality control laboratories.
